blocks.text: A 23-year-old man tells you, calmly and politely, that the newsreader on his television speaks his private thoughts aloud and that a voice in his flat comments on everything he does. Two sentences in, you already have material for three separate parts of the psychiatric examination: a belief, a perception and a pattern of speech. Psychiatry has no scan to read, so the history and the mental state examination are the investigation.

blocks.markdown: The psychiatric assessment has two complementary halves. The **history** is what the patient and others tell you about the course of the illness over time. The **mental state examination (MSE)** is a structured, cross-sectional description of the patient's mental functioning *at the time you see them*, built from what you observe and ask, just as a physical examination records signs. Both are documented in descriptive terms, not by naming a diagnosis, so that another clinician can see the evidence.

### Taking the psychiatric history

Begin with rapport, privacy and open questions, and clarify confidentiality and its limits. Then cover:

- **Presenting complaint** in the patient's own words, and **history of the presenting complaint**: onset, course, stressors, impact on sleep, appetite, work and relationships.
- **Past psychiatric history**: previous episodes, diagnoses, admissions, treatments tried and their effect, self-harm, and any previous use of mental health legislation.
- **Past medical history and medication**: thyroid, neurological and endocrine disease, head injury, epilepsy, and prescribed drugs that can alter mood or cognition (for example steroids).
- **Family history**: psychiatric illness, suicide, substance misuse, and who in the family is a source of support.
- **Personal and developmental history**: pregnancy and birth, milestones, schooling, relationships, occupation, forensic history.
- **Substance history**: alcohol, tobacco, prescribed and illicit drugs, quantity, pattern, route, and dependence features.
- **Social history**: housing, finances, employment, relationships, carers, dependants.
- **Premorbid personality**: how the patient describes themselves and how others describe them.
- **Collateral history** from relatives, carers or records, with appropriate consent, because insight may be limited.

blocks.title: Quantifying alcohol
blocks.text: In the UK one unit is 10 millilitres (8 grams) of pure ethanol. Units of alcohol = volume (ml) x ABV (percent) / 1000. Current UK low-risk guidance advises not regularly drinking more than 14 units a week; confirm against the latest national guidance.

blocks.title: Converting a drinking history into units
blocks.prompt: A patient reports drinking one 500 ml can of cider at 5.0% ABV on each of five weekday evenings, and a 750 ml bottle of wine at 12% ABV on each of two weekend days. Estimate his weekly alcohol intake in units and compare it with the 14-unit low-risk guidance.

steps.text: Units in one can: volume x ABV / 1000.
Units in one bottle of wine.
Weekend total: two bottles, then add the weekday total.
Compare: 30.5 is more than double the 14-unit guideline, so this is hazardous drinking that warrants screening (for example with AUDIT) and exploration of dependence and withdrawal.

blocks.answer: About 30.5 units per week, well above the 14-unit low-risk guidance.

blocks.title: Mental state examination
blocks.text: The MSE is a structured description of the patient's appearance, behaviour, speech, mood and affect, thought (form and content), perception, cognition, and insight and judgement, recorded at a single point in time.

blocks.caption: Components of the mental state examination
rows: Dress, self-care, eye contact, rapport, motor activity, abnormal movements
Unkempt, psychomotor retardation, avoids eye contact
Pressured, rapid; or slow with long pauses
Mood is the patient's sustained subjective state; affect is your observed emotional expression (range, reactivity, congruence)
How thoughts are linked and expressed
Delusions, preoccupations, obsessions, suicidal and violent ideas
Level of consciousness, orientation, attention, memory
Awareness of illness; capacity to make sound decisions
Partial insight; accepts help but doubts diagnosis

blocks.markdown:
### Delusions, hallucinations and thought disorder

Three abnormalities are easily confused because they often occur together in psychosis, but they affect different mental functions.

A **delusion** is a *disorder of thought content*: a fixed, false belief, held with unshakeable conviction despite evidence to the contrary, and out of keeping with the person's culture and background. Themes include persecutory, grandiose, referential (ideas that neutral events carry a special personal meaning), nihilistic, somatic, jealous and erotomanic. A **primary delusion** arises fully formed without explanation; **secondary delusions** arise understandably from another state, such as mood. Passivity phenomena (thought insertion, withdrawal, broadcast, and made actions or feelings) are delusional experiences of external control of the self.

A **hallucination** is a *disorder of perception*: a perception in the absence of an external stimulus, experienced as real, in clear consciousness. It is distinct from an **illusion**, which is a *misperception of a real stimulus* (a coat on a door seen as a person). Auditory hallucinations are typical of schizophrenia (running commentary, third-person voices, commands); visual hallucinations should prompt consideration of an organic cause such as delirium, intoxication or withdrawal, or neurological disease.

**Formal thought disorder** is a *disorder of the form of thought*, inferred from speech: the way ideas are connected rather than what they are. Examples are **loosening of associations or derailment** (the sentences slide off the track, linked by no logical connection), **tangentiality** (replies are oblique), **flight of ideas** (rapid, fragmented but understandable links, often by rhyme or association, typical of mania), **circumstantiality** (excessive detail before returning to the point), **thought block** (sudden interruption), **neologisms** and **word salad**.

blocks.caption: Delusion, hallucination and thought disorder compared
rows: Fixed false belief held with conviction
Illogical or disorganised linking of ideas
Ask about beliefs and explore evidence
Ask about voices, visions and other experiences
Listen to the pattern of spontaneous speech
'The neighbours have bugged my pillow to track me'
Hearing a voice commenting on actions when alone
Sentences that leap between unrelated topics

blocks.title: Labelling abnormal experiences in a transcript
blocks.prompt: A 31-year-old woman says: 'The lights flicker in a pattern meant just for me, so I know the agency is watching. When I'm in the kitchen I hear a man's voice say 'she's washing the plate' although nobody is there. Pencils, windows, the pavement: it all connects.' Classify each experience and state what it is a disorder of.

steps.text: Flickering lights as a coded message for her: she attributes personal meaning to a neutral real event, and holds the belief that an agency is watching without doubt. This is a delusion of reference (with persecutory content), a disorder of thought content.
A man's voice commenting on her actions, heard when nobody is there: a perception without a stimulus, so a third-person running-commentary auditory hallucination, a disorder of perception.

The final utterance links unrelated objects with no clear logical thread: this suggests a loosening of associations, a disorder of thought form. Because only one short sample is given, confirm it across a longer period of spontaneous speech.
Check consciousness and exclude organic causes (substances, delirium, epilepsy) before attributing this to a primary psychotic illness.

blocks.answer: Delusion of reference (thought content), auditory hallucination (perception) and possible loosening of associations (thought form).

blocks.title: Describe, do not diagnose
blocks.text: In an MSE write what you observed: 'speech was rapid and pressured, with rhymes and rapid switching between topics', not 'manic'. Report mood in the patient's own words and affect in your own. Always record suicidal ideation, and your assessment of insight and judgement.

points: The history covers presenting complaint, past psychiatric and medical, family, personal, substance and social history, premorbid personality and collateral information.
The MSE is a cross-sectional description of appearance and behaviour, speech, mood and affect, thought form and content, perception, cognition, insight and judgement.
Delusions are disorders of thought content, hallucinations of perception, formal thought disorder of thought form; illusions are misperceptions of real stimuli.
Alcohol units = volume (ml) x ABV (percent) / 1000, used to compare intake with national low-risk guidance.

questions.stem: During a mental state examination a patient says, 'I know my doctors are impostors replaced by lookalikes', and no amount of evidence changes this. Which MSE domain does this abnormality belong to?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a fixed false belief is a delusion, a disorder of content.
distractorRationale.b: Form concerns how ideas are linked, not what is believed.
distractorRationale.d: Affect is the observed emotional expression.

questions.explanation: A fixed, false, unshakeable belief is a delusion, which is recorded under thought content. Thought form would describe the logical linking of ideas in speech.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man in the evening sees a coat on the bedroom door and, for a moment, believes it is an intruder; when the light is switched on he recognises it as a coat. What is this phenomenon?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: misperception of a real stimulus that corrects on closer inspection.
distractorRationale.b: A hallucination has no external stimulus.
distractorRationale.c: Delusional perception involves a real percept given a false, fixed meaning.
distractorRationale.d: Thought insertion is a passivity experience.

questions.explanation: An illusion is a misinterpretation of an actual stimulus and typically resolves with better lighting or attention. A hallucination would persist without any real stimulus present.

questions.stem: A woman with mania talks very rapidly; each sentence connects to the last by a rhyme or a similar-sounding word, so that the listener can follow the links but the conversation never reaches a point. What is the best description of this speech?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: rapid, understandable associations linked by rhyme or clang, typical of mania.
distractorRationale.b: Thought block is a sudden stop in the flow.
distractorRationale.c: Circumstantiality includes excessive detail but a return to the point.
distractorRationale.d: Poverty of speech is reduced amount.

questions.explanation: Flight of ideas is rapid, pressured speech with associative links that are still followable, often by sound or rhyme. In contrast to schizophrenic derailment, the links are comprehensible.

questions.stem: Which of the following is recorded as 'affect' rather than 'mood' in a mental state examination?

options.text: The clinician's observation that the patient's expression was flat and unreactive
The patient's statement that she feels 'low'
The patient's sustained feeling over the last two weeks
The patient's score on a self-rated questionnaire

questions.correctOptionText: The clinician's observation that the patient's expression was flat and unreactive

distractorRationale.a: Correct: affect is observed emotional expression.
distractorRationale.c: A sustained subjective state is mood.
distractorRationale.d: A questionnaire records subjective report, i.e. mood.

questions.explanation: Mood is the subjective, sustained emotional state reported by the patient, while affect is the objective moment-to-moment emotional expression that the examiner observes, including its range and reactivity.

questions.stem: A patient reports drinking six 330 ml bottles of 5% ABV lager each day, seven days a week. Calculate his weekly alcohol intake (units: UK units per week) using units = volume (ml) x ABV (percent) / 1000.
questions.explanation: One bottle is 330 x 5 / 1000 = 1.65 units, so six bottles is 9.9 units a day and seven days gives 69.3 units a week. This is far above the 14-unit low-risk guidance and should prompt assessment for dependence and withdrawal risk.

questions.stem: During a substance history, a 28-year-old man says he smokes cannabis. Which set of details is most useful to record?

options.text: Amount, frequency, route, age at first use, last use, and any features of dependence or harm
Only whether he has ever tried it

questions.correctOptionText: Amount, frequency, route, age at first use, last use, and any features of dependence or harm

distractorRationale.a: Correct: quantity, pattern and consequences guide risk and relevance to symptoms.
distractorRationale.d: Not required for clinical assessment and unhelpful to rapport.

questions.explanation: A substance history quantifies pattern and consequences so that you can judge dependence and the likely contribution to symptoms such as psychosis or anxiety. Non-judgemental questioning preserves rapport.

questions.stem: True or false: A patient who hears a voice commenting on his actions when nobody is present is experiencing an illusion.
questions.explanation: Hearing a voice with no corresponding external stimulus is an auditory hallucination, and a commentary on one's actions is characteristic of schizophrenia. An illusion would require a real sound that was misinterpreted.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman is admitted with fluctuating alertness, disorientation and vivid visions of small animals on the bed. Which approach to her mental state examination is most appropriate?

options.text: Record the level of consciousness, attention and orientation and consider an organic cause of the visual hallucinations before assuming a primary psychotic disorder
Record only the content of the hallucinations because cognition is outside the MSE
Diagnose schizophrenia because visual hallucinations are typical
Defer the examination until she is fully alert in a month

questions.correctOptionText: Record the level of consciousness, attention and orientation and consider an organic cause of the visual hallucinations before assuming a primary psychotic disorder

distractorRationale.a: Correct: cognition and consciousness are part of the MSE, and visual hallucinations suggest an organic cause.
distractorRationale.b: Cognition is part of the MSE.
distractorRationale.c: Visual hallucinations with clouded consciousness point to delirium, not schizophrenia.
distractorRationale.d: Delay risks missing a treatable cause.

questions.explanation: The cognitive component of the MSE, including consciousness and attention, identifies delirium. Visual hallucinations with fluctuating alertness should prompt a search for an organic cause rather than a primary psychotic diagnosis.

questions.stem: List the main components of a mental state examination and explain how mood differs from affect. Give one example finding for each of two components of your choice.
markingGuide: Mood is the patient's sustained subjective emotional state; affect is the objectively observed expression
Two appropriate worked examples of findings
questions.explanation: The MSE is a cross-sectional systematic description organised under standard headings. Distinguishing mood from affect captures the difference between self-report and observation.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is referred with low mood and poor sleep. Explain what a complete psychiatric history should include, and why a collateral history and a substance history are particularly important in this case.
markingGuide: Presenting complaint and history of presenting complaint in patient's words
Past psychiatric history including self-harm, treatments and admissions
Past medical history and current medication
Family history, personal and developmental history, forensic and social history
Substance history with quantity and pattern, as alcohol and drugs cause or worsen mood and sleep problems
Collateral history for corroboration, especially if insight is limited, with consent and confidentiality considered
questions.explanation: A complete history places the current problem in the person's life and past and identifies causes and risks. Substance use may cause the presentation, and collateral accounts check accuracy when insight or recall is affected.
